title: An LLM workflow that reproduces, improves, extends published economics research
content:
An LLM Workflow That Reproduces, Improves, and Extends Published Economics Research
We introduce an open-source workflow that enables an LLM to reproduce, improve, and extend an economics article using the article’s published replication package. First, the workflow attempts to reproduce the original calculations, checks for discrepancies with published findings, and performs automated sensitivity analysis. Across 4,452 published replication packages for five economics journals, the workflow flags discrepancies in 3,460 articles or their appendices. Second, the workflow improves the original calculations by using a different implementation or algorithm. In 496 articles, the workflow is able to reduce a calculation’s computation time, at similar or greater accuracy, by more than a factor of 10. Third, the workflow extends the original analysis. In 923 articles, the workflow develops an extension that does not appear in the original article and that is aligned with the original article’s goals and assumptions.
- 
      Copy CitationMatthew Schwartz, Isaiah Andrews, and Jesse M. Shapiro, "An LLM Workflow That Reproduces, Improves, and Extends Published Economics Research," NBER Working Paper 35782 (2026), https://doi.org/10.3386/w35782.Download Citation

report.summary: An open-source LLM workflow audits 4,452 economics replication packages, flagging discrepancies in 3,460 and automatically improving or extending hundreds of published analyses.
report.background: Economics and other social sciences have embraced replication packages—code and data deposited with papers—but computational reproducibility remains uneven. Journals require archives, yet code can break across software versions, undocumented steps, and environment differences. Manual reproduction is labor-intensive and rarely done at scale. Meanwhile, LLM coding agents have become capable of reading code, running tests, debugging, and modifying pipelines. This paper tests whether such an agentic workflow can operate on published replication packages end-to-end: reproduce original calculations, compare with published results, run sensitivity checks, optimize algorithms, and propose new extensions. The work sits at the intersection of metascience, automated software engineering, and AI-for-science. If reliable, it could shift peer review and post-publication audit from sporadic manual checks to continuous automated screening. But flagged discrepancies are not automatically errors; they require expert adjudication. The scale—4,452 packages across five journals—makes it a notable stress test of LLM agents on real research code rather than toy benchmarks.
key_points: The workflow examined 4,452 replication packages from five economics journals and flagged discrepancies in 3,460 articles or appendices. At this scale, automated reproduction could become routine screening. But flags need human review: discrepancies may stem from environment changes, data versions, or documentation gaps rather than wrong findings.

In 496 articles, the workflow found a different implementation or algorithm that cut a calculation’s computation time by more than 10x with similar or greater accuracy. This shows LLMs can optimize research code, not just rerun it. It could lower the cost of sensitivity analyses and large reruns, but optimized code still needs validation.

In 923 articles, the workflow generated an extension not present in the original but aligned with its goals and assumptions. This moves from reproducibility toward automated research assistance. It raises questions about novelty, attribution, and whether such extensions are substantively meaningful rather than merely plausible.

The authors released an open-source workflow that lets an LLM use a paper’s published replication package. Journals, replicators, and developers could adapt it. But LLM nondeterminism, API costs, data-access restrictions, software licensing, and audit trails will shape whether it becomes trustworthy infrastructure.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a concrete demonstration of agentic LLM workflows operating on messy, real-world scientific code—useful for benchmarking coding agents beyond toy tasks. For developers, the open-source workflow offers a template for sandboxed code execution, output comparison, optimization, and extension generation, though reliability, cost, and reproducibility of the LLM itself remain challenges. For regular users, automated audits could surface unreliable economics evidence faster and make published findings more transparent, but false alarms and overreliance on LLM judgments are real risks. Journals may move toward continuous computational screening, while researchers face more scrutiny and new norms around documenting code, environments, and AI-assisted extensions. Human expert review remains essential before any discrepancy is treated as an error.
report.tools: Watch the authors’ open-source workflow (NBER Working Paper 35782), NBER replication archives, and LLM coding agents such as OpenHands, Aider, and SWE-agent. For reproducible environments, use Docker, Conda, and Snakemake; for archiving, Zenodo or Code Ocean. To try it, pick a small replication package, run the original code in a sandbox, log software versions, compare outputs, then test one targeted optimization—always with human review.
